claims.text: Untreated CoCrFeNi exhibits temperature-dependent increases in friction and wear.
The increased friction and wear of untreated CoCrFeNi are caused by uncontrolled oxidation and surface degradation.
A tailored surface treatment can create an adaptive layer that forms a continuous, self-healing oxide tribofilm during sliding.
The in-situ oxide tribofilm adheres to the alloy surface and minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide tribofilm dynamically adapts its structure through self-healing and controlled oxidation as temperature and load change.
During sliding, the engineered surface layer reacts with ambient oxygen in a controlled manner to form an oxide tribofilm.
The tribofilm acts as a lubricious, protective interface that reduces adhesive wear.
Controlled tribofilm formation prevents crack-prone, uncontrolled oxide layers from governing sliding damage.
Self-healing keeps the tribofilm intact under variable thermal and mechanical loads.
Surface-engineered CoCrFeNi will have a consistently lower coefficient of friction than untreated CoCrFeNi from room temperature to 800 °C.
Surface-engineered CoCrFeNi will have a reduced specific wear rate relative to untreated CoCrFeNi from room temperature to 800 °C.
The friction and wear improvements will persist as normal load and oxygen availability are varied.
Extreme loads may compromise the effectiveness of the intervention.
Environments that inhibit controlled oxidation may compromise the intervention.
A controlled comparison of treated and untreated CoCrFeNi across temperature, load, and oxygen conditions can test the hypothesis using friction, wear, and tribofilm measurements.

Failure to obtain statistically significant friction and wear reductions across all test conditions, together with an absent, discontinuous, or non-self-healing tribofilm, would falsify the hypothesis.
